item.title: ‘Who knows what’s gonna happen’: Canada, U.S. residents weigh in on latest trade talks
item.description: Canadians and Americans visiting Niagara Falls, Ont., are voicing both cautious hope and deep skepticism over a looming trade deal between the two countries.
item.dc:creator: Heather Wright
item.content:encoded: NIAGARA FALLS, Ont. – Canadians and Americans visiting Niagara Falls, Ont., are voicing both cautious hope and deep skepticism over a looming trade deal between the two countries. “I think the whole thing is kind of ridiculous,” said Massachusetts resident Hannah Herrera. “We should have a good relationship with Canada, and … it’s really sad that it’s come to this, but we hope that it’s over soon.” John Herrera echoes his wife’s opinion but is less optimistic that a deal will hold. “I hope it’s over and I hope it doesn’t happen again, but we’ve gone through this multiple times,” John Herrera said. Canadian Chuck Henderson is also skeptical, noting that U.S. President Donald Trump has reversed course in the past when it comes to tariffs. “He goes one way one day, and then three weeks later, he goes, ‘oh that was the worst deal ever,’” Henderson said. “So, who knows what’s gonna happen.” With the cost of living high in both countries, some visitors are hopeful a deal could ease financial pressure. “The price of everything has gone up, so yeah, we definitely would prefer if our government made some different choices,” said Adrienne Forken, an American from Rochester, N.Y. Experts say concessions in any deal are inevitable, which according to Montreal resident Louis Fachimi, sounds like a reasonable trade-off. “Maybe we should give some concessions, and they give some concessions, and we can get some middle term to end this battle,” he said. Others though worry about how much Canada might have to give up, and whether American products produced with lower standards will be allowed into the Canadian market. “We’ve got the right guy in charge to get us a better deal than we would’ve gotten otherwise,” said Elizabeth Wenniock of Newmarket, Ont., referring to Prime Minister Mark Carney. “But yeah, we need to stand firm on all of our standards to keep them high.” Even with a deal appearing imminent, many Canadians at the Falls said they’d be fine with the government continuing to fight for the country’s interests. “If it doesn’t work for both of us, then let’s not do it,” said Mary McIntyre. “We don’t wanna play this administration’s game. (Trump’s) toxic as far as I’m concerned.” Marva Campbell says Canadians should keep fighting to stand up for its interests and values. “We can fight,” she said. “We are Canadians and we’re not fighting. I think we can do more. We have more power than we actually use,” she said. But after roughly 18 months of trade turmoil, people like John Dickinson of Newmarket are simply fed up. “Just play like nice children in the sandbox,” he said.

item.title: Canada, U.S. both say they made gains in new trade deal that averted tariffs
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney is scheduled to brief his cabinet and Canada’s premiers today about the trade deal reached with the United States on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Canada-U.S. Minister Dominic LeBlanc smiled widely beside U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade czar in Washington on Wednesday as they touted a draft deal which appears to have averted a new round of punishing tariffs on Canada. United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he feels confident the agreement will protect American workers and jobs while strengthening the North American market, making the continent a manufacturing and energy powerhouse. “We certainly, I think, have eliminated some of the irritants that we’ve had over the past year,” he said, “We also are taking a strong foot forward.” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that the new deal reinforces and builds on Canada’s existing trade advantages with the U.S.  LeBlanc and Greer had their latest meeting the morning after Trump announced a three-day pause on 50 per cent tariffs that were set to slam an array of Canadian goods just after midnight Wednesday. LeBlanc did not provide many details about the specifics of the draft agreement he had hammered out with Greer during weeks of heightened negotiations. He did say Canada’s dairy supply managed system would remain intact. Multiple news reports have said the deal will see the United States lower sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum. Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal both reported the duties would be reduced from the current 50 per cent levels to 25 per cent. A source with knowledge of some terms of the agreement but who is authorized to speak publicly about them told The Canadian Press that lower duties on steel and aluminum were part of the deal but could not say how the tariff rate would change. LeBlanc returned to Ottawa Wednesday to meet with Carney and hold other meetings to put finishing touches on Canada’s side of the trade negotiations.  Greer said he will brief Congress and American stakeholders on what the two sides have been talking about.  Canada-U.S. Minister Dominic LeBlanc smiled widely beside U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade czar in Washington on Wednesday as they touted a draft deal which appears to have averted a new round of punishing tariffs on Canada. LeBlanc did not provide many details about the specifics of the draft agreement he had hammered out with Greer during weeks of heightened negotiations. He did say Canada’s dairy supply managed system would remain intact. Multiple news reports have said the deal will see the United States lower sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum. Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal both reported the duties would be reduced from the current 50 per cent levels to 25 per cent. A source with knowledge of some terms of the agreement but who is authorized to speak publicly about them told The Canadian Press that lower duties on steel and aluminum were part of the deal but could not say how the tariff rate would change. LeBlanc returned to Ottawa Wednesday to meet with Carney and hold other meetings to put finishing touches on Canada’s side of the trade negotiations.  Greer said he will brief Congress and American stakeholders on what the two sides have been talking about.  Members of the prime minister’s advisory council on Canada-U.S. relations, who were briefed about the deal Tuesday night, welcomed the tariff pause but said uncertainty continues to harm Canadian businesses. Lana Payne, Unifor national president, said the “devil is going to be in the details” of the agreement.  Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party was relieved to hear there was a deal in the works but repeated his claim that any agreement must include zero tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber as well as an exemption to the “Buy America” policies. The deal could come together by Trump’s latest deadline, said William Pellerin, a partner in international trade at McMillan LLP in Ottawa.  Unlike CUSMA negotiations, Pellerin said this would amount to adjustments to tariffs on the margins — those rates and retaliatory measures can be adjusted with letters, executive orders in the U.S. or an order-in-council on the Canadian side. But Pellerin also cautioned that there’s very little Canada can do at this stage to hold the United States to its word. He noted Trump has gone back on tariff deals struck with other countries. “We have to understand that any deal that we strike could get overturned and that we’re buying temporary relief,” Pellerin said. By Kelly Geraldine Malone With files from David Baxter, Craig Lord, Catherine Morrison and Sarah Ritchie in Ottawa

item.title: An alarmed bond market gets the Trump administration to act again
item.description: The bond market can occasionally send warning signals loud enough to hit stock markets worldwide and even grab the attention of world leaders.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Normally quiet, the bond market can occasionally send warning signals loud enough to hit stock markets worldwide and even grab the attention of U.S. presidents and other world leaders. After the bond market’s alarm bells rose in volume through the summer, the Trump administration announced on Wednesday a move that could help calm it down. The U.S. Treasury Department said it will more than double the amount of U.S. government bonds that it will buy back, and the move worked in getting longer-term yields lower, for now at least. Yields worldwide had earlier climbed to heights not reached in years and, in some cases, decades, because of the jump in oil prices due to the war with Iran, worries about big and growing debts for governments and other concerns. The stakes are high because high yields drag on economies and bring downward pressure on stock markets after Wall Street hit records on excitement about big corporate profits and the promise of artificial-intelligence technology. But what’s to come is still uncertain, and some analysts warn the Treasury Department’s move could even ultimately backfire. Here’s a look at what’s going on and how things got this way: Bond yields have been rising In the United States, the centerpiece of the bond market recently touched its highest yield in more than a year. The 10-year Treasury yield, which shows how much interest investors want the U.S. government to pay them before they’ll lend it money for a decade, topped 4.70 per cent, before falling back to 4.65 per cent Wednesday. That’s up from just 3.97 per cent before the Iran war began in late February, and it’s a significant move for the bond market. More notably, the 30-year U.S. Treasury yield has jumped well above 5 per cent, back to where it was in 2007, before the 2008 financial crisis sent yields crashing toward zero worldwide. In Japan, the yield on the 10-year government bond has touched its highest level in nearly 30 years, while the German 10-year yield is back to where it was in 2011. High yields can slow the economy When the U.S. and other governments have to pay more in interest to borrow money, so do people and companies. For many U.S. households, that’s most easily seen through rates for mortgages. Such rates have climbed with the 10-year Treasury yield since the Iran war began, and the average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage is near its highest level in a year. Higher yields also make it more expensive for U.S. companies to borrow money to build factories and otherwise grow. That’s particularly dangerous at this moment, when big investments in data centers to power AI are a major driver of the U.S. economy’s growth. High yields affect all kinds of investments If high yields slow the economy, that puts pressure on the stocks. An economic slowdown would threaten how much profit companies can make, which is the lifeblood of the stock market. High yields undercut the stock market in other ways too. When a Treasury is paying more in interest, that can draw investors away from investments that carry more risk. Why pay record prices for U.S. stocks when a U.S. government bond is paying more than before to wait in relative safety? Gold, bitcoin and many other investments can also feel downward pressure from high yields. Then there’s the impact on the government When yields rise, the U.S. and other governments have to pay more in interest to cover their debts. That’s painful when debt loads for governments worldwide are ballooning as they spend far more than they’re bringing in through revenue. And if the U.S. government is already paying this much to borrow money when the economy is growing, what will happen if it needs to borrow even more to manage the pain when the next severe recession hits? That’s why jumps in yields can scare politicians even more than swings in the stock market. The bond market helped make Liz Truss the United Kingdom’s shortest-serving prime minister in 2022, when it revolted against her plan to cut taxes and raise spending without a way to pay for them. Last year, U.S. President Donald Trump said the bond market may have played a role in his decision to delay many of his proposed tariffs, saying that he noticed investors there “were getting a little queasy.” The long-term effect of the U.S. Treasury department’s move is uncertain U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s move is a high-stakes effort to contain the rise in long-term yields, and some analysts are skeptical the impact will last. “The operation changes almost nothing in terms of the fundamentals, in particular the unchanged need to finance the tidal wave of hyperscaler debt in addition to very large government deficits,” Krishna Guha, an analyst at Evercore ISI, and colleagues wrote in a note to clients. “Hyperscalers” refers to the Big Tech companies that are borrowing mountains of money to build AI data centers. The bonds they’re selling are competing with U.S. Treasurys for buyers, which can push bond yields higher. The U.S. government, meanwhile, continues to run its own large deficits regardless of what the Treasury Department does with its repurchases. “The move could even backfire if the limited firepower results in little sustained impact,” Guha said. A rate cut by the U.S. Federal Reserve won’t magically solve the problem The Federal Reserve could always cut the federal funds rate, which affects very short-term, overnight loans. But longer-term yields like the 10- and 30-year Treasury yields are set by investors in the bond market. And recently, they have been demanding more in interest to make up for the growing risks of high inflation, continued government deficits and other factors. The Fed also appears more likely to raise its benchmark short-term rate than to cut it. At its last meeting in late July, three Fed policymakers voted to raise the fed funds rates even as nine voted to keep it unchanged. And Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s decision to signal little about the Fed’s next moves appeared to push longer-term Treasury yields higher amid questions about what the central bank will do to get inflation back to its 2 per cent target. The government’s most recent inflation data suggest inflation may be slowing, leading many on Wall Street to forecast the Fed will keep the federal funds rates steady at its next meeting in September. The next big potentially market-moving event may come on Aug. 28, when Warsh will give a speech at the Fed’s annual economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. --- Stan Choe And Christopher Rugaber, The Associated Press

item.title: Why is Trump talking about the Keystone XL pipeline?
item.description: Trump is talking about the project again five years after it was shut down by Biden when he was president. Here's everything you need to know.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. President Donald Trump hinted that he may revive an old pipeline project that would export oil from Canada to the U.S. as part of a pending trade deal. In a Truth Social post shared Tuesday night, Trump said he had suspended the 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods for three days , two hours before they were set to take place on Wednesday.

The deal, he stated, may include revitalizing the Keystone XL pipeline, a long hotly-contested project that has been in the works for almost a decade. Trump had attempted to revive the project during his first presidency as part of his then-campaign promises, but the pipeline was quashed by Joe Biden in the first year of his term. “The great Keystone XL Pipeline, long ago killed by Sleepy Joe Biden, may be awoken from the grave!” Trump’s social media post reads . He then published an AI-generated image of himself hoisting the Keystone XL pipeline out of a gravesite marked by a tombstone labelled “BURIED BY BIDEN.” Donald Trump tariffs on Canada Prime Minister Carney did not mention the pipeline in his own statement on Trump’s announcement. “Substantial progress has been made, although there is important work still to be done,” read the statement. First proposed in 2008, the project has seen a rocky journey, piled with legal barriers, opposition from environmental and Indigenous activists, and subject to the whims of U.S presidents at different points in time. What is Keystone XL? It has been proposed as an expansion project that would carry Canadian crude oil to the U.S. Gulf Coast and, if built, potentially increase those exports to the U.S. by more than 12 per cent. The current Keystone pipeline, first proposed in 2005 and built between 2008 and 2010, runs from Hardisty, Alta., across Saskatchewan and Manitoba and before crossing the U.S. near Haskett, Man., into North Dakota, Illinois and Nebraska . Keystone XL, if it had gone ahead, would have seen a direct route built between Hardisty and Steele City, Neb. However, only the U.S. portions of the extension have been constructed so far. Trump hinted at reviving the Keystone XL expansion project in his social media post on Tuesday night, five years after it was put to bed by Joe Biden. (The Associated Press) Trump hinted at reviving the Keystone XL expansion project in his social media post on Tuesday night, five years after it was put to bed by Joe Biden. (The Associated Press) How was it initially approved? The project was first proposed in 2008 by its then-owners TC Energy Corp. and ConocoPhilips. At the time, TC Energy Corp. was called TransCanada Corp. The Canadian Energy Board approved the project in 2010, but that came with 22 conditions on safety, environmental protection and landowner rights. Then-U.S. president Barack Obama was the first to shut it down two years later, in January 2012. Former U.S. President Barack Obama waves to the crowd following a speech before the Montreal Board of Trade Tuesday, June 6, 2017 in Montreal. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Paul Chiasson Former U.S. president Barack Obama waves to the crowd following a speech before the Montreal Board of Trade Tuesday, June 6, 2017, in Montreal. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Paul Chiasson Why is it so controversial? The project has seen major opposition from legislators and activists, citing environmental concerns, lack of legal oversight and unconstitutional use of state law to review the routes. Obama rejected the project in 2012 after U.S. legislators passed a bill in December 2011 that stated the president had to make a decision on the pipeline’s future in 60 days. Obama argued that this did not allow much time to review the new route but said TransCanada was free to submit another application. Between 2012 and 2016 , project costs ballooned as TransCanada looked to build southern legs of the expansion. While the company found favour in the Nebraska state government and a Republican-led U.S. Congress, the project was repeatedly shot down through legal challenges from pipeline opponents and a veto from the Obama administration. AM800-NEWS-DONALD-TRUMP-MICHIGAN-GETTY-1.2168036 Then-Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump addresses supporters during a campaign rally on Nov. 8, 2016, in Grand Rapids, Michigan. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images) Trump, in his 2016 presidential campaign, vowed to bring back the project if elected. In January 2017, he signed an executive order approving the project with plans to renegotiate the terms. The project still faced legal challenges over the next two years with construction getting underway in April 2020. In November, Biden was elected president and shut down the project on his first day of presidency. Why did Biden cancel the project? Biden cancelled the project in January 2021 , stating that it did not align with his administration ’s economic and environmental objectives. He had served as U.S. vice-president during the Obama administration. President Joe Biden speaks during a Department of Defense Commander in Chief farewell ceremony at Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall, Jan. 16, 2025, in Arlington, Va. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci, File) U.S. President Joe Biden speaks during a Department of Defense Commander in Chief farewell ceremony at Joint Base Myer-Henderson Hall, Jan. 16, 2025, in Arlington, Va. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci, File) Then-Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau expressed disappointment over the cancellation and stated that his representatives were pressing the Biden administration to reconsider. Then-Alberta premier Jason Kenney threatened legal action if the project was scrapped. What has happened since? The project remained buried until Trump entered his second term as president. In February 2025, Trump posted on social media that he wanted to revive the Keystone XL project. In October, Carney pitched the project to Trump in exchange for relief from U.S. steel and aluminum tariffs on Canada’s industries, to which Trump was “very receptive,” according to media reports published then . In March, Alberta Liberal MP Corey Hogan confirmed that the pipeline was being used as leverage in trade talks with the U.S. “As we start thinking about some of the exposed industries and some of those that are really being hit hard by tariffs, we’ve got to have things to negotiate with, and energy is one of those things,” Hogan told CTV’s Power Play at the time. He added it would be “foolish” for the federal government not to “think about the opportunities” the pipeline project could provide. While the pipeline did not appear to be part of the pending trade deal, it could become a “sticking point” for Trump, according to CTV News political analyst Eric Ham. He told CTV News Channel on Wednesday that the situation seems “mysterious,” but noted Trump has prioritized “oil and energy” as a key component in his administration and in negotiations with Canada and other countries. “We saw how the president was willing to invade, frankly, Venezuela over energy,” Ham said. “So this has always been a priority.” Related Stories Industry experts see ‘steep barriers’ to Keystone XL revival Opens in new window Keystone XL ‘one of the cards’ Canada has in U.S. trade negotiations: Liberal MP Opens in new window
